summary: Defines message encipherment and authentication procedures as the first phase of privacy enhancement for Internet electronic mail. Detailed key management was left to a later RFC. It aims to work with symmetric and public-key approaches. It replaces RFC 989 and was replaced by RFC 1113.

eli5.summary: It explains how to lock an email in a box and sign it so only the right person can open it and they know it came from you.

questions: how to encrypt and authenticate email messages
how does privacy enhanced mail work
how does pem handle multiple recipients
what are data encrypting keys and interchange keys
subtitle: The first part of a privacy enhancement system for email that encrypts and authenticates messages.

tldr.problem: Email on the Internet travels in plaintext and lacks proof of who sent it, making it vulnerable to eavesdropping and forgery.
tldr.mechanism: PEM adds cryptographic layers to email: messages are encrypted with one-time data keys, the keys themselves are encrypted with interchange keys held by sender and recipient, and integrity checks are added so recipients can verify messages have not been altered.
tldr.outcome: It provided a framework for private and authenticated email that worked across the Internet without requiring changes to mail servers or central authorities, though later efforts like SMIME eventually became more widely adopted.

facts.label: Encryption algorithm
facts.value: DEA-1 (Data Encryption Standard) in CBC mode

today: RFC 1040 was obsoleted by RFC 1113 and related RFCs that refined the PEM framework. While PEM was an important pioneering effort in email security, it was eventually superseded by S/MIME and other approaches that achieved broader adoption.

sections.title: Privacy Enhancement for Electronic Mail
sections.content:
RFC 1040 defines the first part of a system called Privacy Enhanced Mail (PEM) that adds encryption and authentication to Internet email. Written by the IAB Privacy Task Force, it describes message encipherment and authentication procedures. The RFC aims to work with both symmetric (shared-secret) and public-key cryptography approaches, though detailed key management is left to follow-on RFCs.

The system is designed so that privacy enhancement is applied end-to-end between sender and recipient, with no special processing required from intermediate mail servers. This allows privacy features to be added gradually, site by site and user by user, without disrupting the existing Internet mail infrastructure.
sections.eli5: This RFC explains how to make email private and signed. The idea is that you and the person you're emailing can add encryption and signatures without needing special permission from anyone in between.

sections.title: The Two-Level Encryption System
sections.content:
PEM uses two different types of cryptographic keys working together. Data Encrypting Keys (DEKs) encrypt the message itself. A new DEK is generated randomly for each message, so no single key protects multiple messages. The DEK is then encrypted for transmission using Interchange Keys (IKs), which are longer-lived keys shared between a sender-recipient pair. A message carries one copy of the encrypted DEK for each recipient.

This two-level approach means the sender and recipient must first share an interchange key, but the key management system can be flexible: keys might be distributed by a central server, agreed between users directly, or obtained through other means. The RFC intentionally leaves detailed key management to later documents.
sections.eli5: You use two sets of keys: a different throwaway key for each message (DEK), and a long-term key you share with each person (IK). The message key is locked with the long-term key, so only that person can unlock it.

sections.title: Message Transformations and Encoding
sections.content:
Messages go through a series of transformations to ensure they can be encrypted, verified, and transmitted reliably across different computer systems. First, the plaintext message in its native local format is converted to a canonical form equivalent to standard SMTP representation (ASCII character set with CR-LF line endings). This step ensures that when the message reaches a different type of computer, the encryption and integrity check will still work.

Next, the canonical message is authenticated by computing a Message Integrity Check (MIC) code. Selected portions of the message are then encrypted using DEA-1 (the Data Encryption Standard) in CBC mode. Finally, the encrypted bytes are encoded into a printable form using a 64-character alphabet similar to Base64, with two special characters to mark boundaries of unencrypted regions. This encoding ensures the encrypted message passes safely through SMTP systems that might reject binary data.
sections.eli5: The message gets converted to a standard format, then locked up, then converted to a form of text that any mail system can handle without breaking it.

sections.title: Message Encapsulation and Control Headers
sections.content:
Privacy-enhanced messages are wrapped in an encapsulation structure that preserves the original message while adding cryptographic control information. The structure includes an outer header (standard mail headers), a blank line, a pre-encapsulation boundary marker, an encapsulated header with control fields, another blank line, the encoded message text, and a post-encapsulation boundary marker.

The encapsulated header fields carry cryptographic information: X-Proc-Type identifies the version, X-IV carries the initialization vector for encryption, X-Sender-ID identifies the sender's key, X-Recipient-ID identifies each recipient's key, and X-Key-Info carries the encrypted DEK and MIC for each recipient. Additional fields like X-Certificate carry public-key certificates when asymmetric cryptography is used. This encapsulation approach allows privacy enhancement to be applied recursively and works with mail systems that only handle text, not special header fields.
sections.eli5: The message is wrapped up with special control information that says who sent it, who can read it, and how to unlock it. The wrapping doesn't break the message if it goes through old mail systems.

sections.title: Key Management and Certificates
sections.content:
Each Data Encrypting Key is used only once and can be generated either centrally by key distribution centers or by the sender's system. Centralized generation offers better random number generation but requires trust in the KDC; decentralized generation allows senders to be self-sufficient and reduces dependency on real-time server access.

Interchange Keys are typically managed on a pairwise per-user basis, meaning each pair of users who want to exchange private mail needs a shared IK. For public-key cryptography, a sender has the recipient's public component and the recipient has their own secret component; together these form the interchange key. When public-key management is used, certificates bind a user's public key to their identity in a way verified by a trusted Issuing Authority. The RFC notes that keys can be shared through central servers, direct user agreement, or other mechanisms, leaving these details to follow-on specifications.
sections.eli5: The long-term key is shared between two people somehow—maybe a server hands it out, maybe you and your friend trade it in person. In public-key systems, the certificate proves the key really belongs to that person.
